newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.N. tribunal judges criticise Bosnia conference.
newsitem.headline: U.N. tribunal judges criticise Bosnia conference.

text.p: Judges at the Hague-based U.N. criminal tribunal for former Yugoslavia on Wednesday complained that they had been marginalised at a conference in London called to take stock of the year-old Bosnian peace process.

"The tribunal wishes to express its deep concern that the organisers...have omitted to mention the issue of cooperation with the International Tribunal in the (conference) programme," they said in a statement.
They added that it was "regrettable" the tribunal had been invited to attend the conference only as an observer and not as a participant.
"The (tribunal's) essential role in the restoration of peace and security in Bosnia and Herzegovia...appears to have been down-graded," the statement said.
A tribunal delegation was invited to address the last full Peace Implementation Conference in Florence in June.

The two-day London conference, which began on Wednesday, was expected to criticise Bosnia's various ethnic communities for not sticking to the terms of the Dayton peace agreement which ended the 43-month war in the former Yugoslav republic.
More than 50 national delegations as well as representatives from major aid agencies were attending.

The tribunal judges reminded the conference that the United Nations Security Council approving the Dayton deal, stated that "compliance with the requests and orders of the International Tribunal constitutes an essential aspect of implementing the peace agreement".
"Yet, this essential aspect is not reflected in the programme for the London Peace Conference," the judges said.
The tribunal was set up by the Security Council in 1993 to try those accused of war crimes during Bosnia's bitter ethnic conflict.

It has indicted more than 70 Serbs, Croats and Moslems, including deposed Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and former military chief General Ratko Mladic, but has only seven suspects in its custody.

Authorities in various areas of the former Yugoslavia have given only limited cooperation to the tribunal while NATO forces implementing the Dayton agreement have been loath to hunt down and arrest suspects.
